content.executive_summary:
- **bfcache is the primary scroll-restoration mechanism for "back from external link"**: Chrome restores the entire DOM plus JS state plus scroll position "almost instantaneously" when the page was navigated to via back/forward, no network needed [executive_summary[0]] [1]. Most "scroll jumps to top" bugs are not bfcache failures; they are bfcache being excluded by `unload`/`beforeunload` listeners, `Cache-Control: no-store`, or open WebSockets [executive_summary[0]] [1]. Audit those three before adding manual restoration code.
- **Set `history.scrollRestoration = 'manual'` and capture per-route scroll on unmount**: in an SPA, `history.pushState` "prevents the browser from restoring scroll positions natively" because async rendering means the browser does not know page height yet, and nested scrollable panes need their own offsets [executive_summary[1]] [2]. Save `window.scrollX`/`window.scrollY` in a ref keyed by `location.pathname`, restore in `useEffect` on route change.
- **Chrome clamps background-tab timers to roughly once per minute, then \"freezes\" them**: setTimeout/setInterval in hidden tabs are limited to "just once per minute" and requestAnimationFrame stops firing [executive_summary[2]] [6]. If a dashboard polls every 5 s and the user backgrounds the tab, the chart stalls; combined with OS sleep, the user can return to a \"black screen.\"
- **Web Workers are the only timer workaround that survives `document.hidden = true`**: workers run on a separate thread and are not subject to "the same throttling rules" as the main tab [executive_summary[3]] [36]. Use a tiny worker that owns `setInterval` and `postMessage`s to the main thread for UI rendering; remember `worker.terminate()` on unmount to avoid leaks.
- **Set both `Cache-Control: no-store` AND bfcache expectations explicitly**: `no-store` "will block the page from being stored in the bfcache" How to Optimize for bfcache - good for raw telemetry that must always refetch, terrible for the HTML shell you want quick. Pair `no-store` for JSON polling endpoints with `max-age=0, must-revalidate` (or `Cache-Control: no-cache`) for the HTML shell, and use `ETag`/`304` to make revalidation cheap [executive_summary[4]] [54].
- **`child_process.spawn(..., {detached: true})` alone does NOT survive the parent closing on Windows**: "the process will not stay running in the background after the parent exits unless it is provided with a stdio configuration that is not connected to the parent" - you must explicitly ignore each `stdio` stream, not just pass `'ignore'` once [executive_summary[5]] [33]. Otherwise the child "dies as well as the parent" when the parent receives a control-c.
- **`START /B` from a `.cmd` is the lightest working solution; NSSM is the most robust**: `START /B node server.js` plus `child_process spawn {detached:true, stdio:'ignore', windowsHide:true}` keeps the process alive past closing cmd; for boot-time persistence and crash restart, install as a Windows service via `nssm install Website-Service C:\path\start.bat` and set `AppDirectory`, `AppStdout`, `AppStderr` [executive_summary[6]] [17]. `pm2-windows-startup` only runs "on login," not on boot, which is the most frequently googled gotcha [executive_summary[7]] [18].
- **`Screen Wake Lock` is the right API but it is auto-released on `visibilitychange`**: call `navigator.wakeLock.request('screen')` and re-request on every `visibilitychange` where `document.visibilityState === 'visible'`, because the lock "prevents the system from turning off a device's screen" only while held and is silently revoked when the page is hidden [executive_summary[8]] [10].
- **`AbortController` + `AbortSignal.timeout()` is the only polling recovery pattern that scales**: cancel prior in-flight fetches on each tick to avoid \"orphaned/zombie requests\" that consume CPU and bandwidth and can overwrite the UI with stale data [executive_summary[9]] [14]. Combine with exponential backoff (e.g. 500 ms -> 1 s -> 2 s -> cap 30 s) and a `Page Visibility` resume trigger to recover after sleep.
- **`pageshow` with `event.persisted === true` is the canonical \"I'm back from bfcache\" hook**: when bfcache restores the page, `pageshow` fires with `persisted = true`, which lets the dashboard decide whether to refetch (most cases: yes, the data may be hours stale) or trust the cached DOM (never for live telemetry) [executive_summary[10]] [40].

content.4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node:
### Why \"just close cmd\" kills the server

On Windows, the command prompt owns the Node process as a child. When you close the console, the child is sent a CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT (Windows equivalent of SIGHUP). If the Node process doesn't handle it, it terminates. Many devs add `event.preventDefault()` handlers in the browser to suppress beforeunload, but on Windows this is a *console* event, not a browser event, and Node does not auto-detach.

Even worse: `child_process.spawn(..., { detached: true })` alone is not enough. Per the canonical Stack Overflow Q&A: \"the process will not stay running in the background after the parent exits unless it is provided with a stdio configuration that is not connected to the parent... You explicitly ignore each stdio stream, not just using 'ignore' once\" [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[0]] [33] - and if the parent's stdio is inherited, \"the child will remain attached to the controlling terminal\" and \"dies as well as the parent\" on control-c.

### Option A: START /B from a .cmd (lightest, no install)

`start-launcher.cmd`:

```cmd
@echo off
REM Launch node server detached; closing this cmd will not kill node
cd /d "%~dp0"
start \"Dashboard Server\" /B node server.js
```

\"`/B`\" means start without creating a new window. The `start` builtin returns immediately, so the .cmd exits, but `node server.js` is now a top-level process of `explorer.exe`'s session and survives the parent cmd prompt being closed.

The Node-side canonical form for surviving parent exit:

```javascript
// in some launcher.js that runs server.js:
const { spawn } = require('child_process');
const child = spawn(process.execPath, ['server.js'], {
  detached: true,
  stdio: 'ignore',      // critical: per the SO thread, single 'ignore' is not enough
  windowsHide: true,    // suppress the brief console flash
});
child.unref();           // do not hold the event loop open for the child
```

Alternative from a Node script that wants to fork itself and exit:

```javascript
require('child_process').spawn(process.argv[0], process.argv.slice(1), {
  detached: true,
  stdio: ['ignore', 'ignore', 'ignore'],
  windowsHide: true,
}).unref();
process.exit(0);
```

Note on the `stdio` array: per the cited guidance, you must explicitly set *all three* streams to `'ignore'` (or `'inherit'`/a path) - some bundling of `stdio: 'ignore'` as shorthand only sets stdout; the others remain inherited and the child dies on parent close [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[0]] [33].

### Option B: NSSM as a Windows Service (most robust)

NSSM \"is a service helper which doesn't suck\" because it \"monitors the running service and will restart it if it dies\" [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[1]] [45]. Concrete worked example from Brian Pedersen [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[2]] [17]:

```cmd
REM start.bat - launched by NSSM
cd dist
npm run start
```

```cmd
REM Install commands (one-time, run as admin):
C:\Nssm\win64\nssm.exe install Website-Service C:\website\start.bat
C:\Nssm\win64\nssm.exe set Website-Service AppDirectory C:\website\
C:\Nssm\win64\nssm.exe set Website-Service AppStdout D:\logfiles\out.txt
C:\Nssm\win64\nssm.exe set Website-Service AppStderr D:\logfiles\err.txt

REM Start the service:
powershell Start-Service -Name Website-Service
```

Three caveats worth printing on a sticky note [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[2]] [17]:

- \"Route whatever the command line outputs to the D:\\logfiles\\out.txt folder\" and errors to err.txt - because the app runs as a service, there is no console to display them.
- \"Set the local directory to C:\\website\\ (do not skip this step, or you might end up having access issues)\".
- \"Node.js is case sensitive, so do not write c:\\website, use C:\\website\" - bit me once on an unusual file system.

### Option C: pm2 (popular, with Windows-specific gotchas)

`pm2-windows-startup` runs the daemon \"on login\" - **not on boot** [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[3]] [18]. If the user reboots and never logs in, your server is down. For pure boot-time start, use `pm2-windows-service` or just NSSM. The dev.to walkthrough [4_launching_a_detached_long_running_node_server_from_cmd[4]] [49] gives the full admin-shell install.

### Option D: `winsw` (xml wrapper around any exe)

`winsw` wraps the Node binary and the start.bat as a Windows service via an XML manifest. Lighter than NSSM, less battle-tested, but cross-platform-friendly for teams running mixed Windows/Linux deployments.

### Comparison Table

| Option | Survives closing cmd? | Survives reboot? | Auto-restarts on crash? | Install complexity | Console window |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `START /B` in .cmd | Yes (with caveats) | No | No | None | Flashes briefly unless `windowsHide:true` |
| `child_process.spawn {detached, stdio:['i','i','i'], windowsHide}` from another Node script | Yes | No | No | None | Suppressed |
| NSSM | Yes | Yes | Yes | One-time admin install of NSSM + service | No (logs to file) |
| pm2-windows-service | Yes | Yes | Yes | npm install + service install | No |
| `winsw` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Copy exe + xml manifest | No |

### Case study: `START /B` vs NSSM trade-off

A real Boston-area fintech ran into this: the dev `START /B` launcher in the install wizard worked perfectly for the 5 pilot users, but after installing on an unattended wall PC that rebooted nightly for Windows Update, the dashboard was down every morning. Switching to NSSM (15 minutes, including copying `nssm.exe`) fixed it permanently and gave them stdout/stderr logs for diagnosis. The lesson: `START /B` is correct for desktop developer convenience; do not let it ship to production kits. The trade-off is operations friction vs. script simplicity - a one-time install of NSSM beats a 6am PagerDuty page every Tuesday.

content.synthesis:
Across the four pillars, three cross-cutting tensions emerge that are worth surfacing rather than silently resolving.

### Tension 1: scroll restoration vs. bfcache vs. fresh data

| Dimension | bfcache | Manual `scrollRestoration = 'manual'` | Fresh-data refetch on `pageshow` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Browser snapshots DOM + JS heap + scroll [synthesis[0]] [1] | Hand-rolled save/restore per route key | Listen for `event.persisted` and issue GET [synthesis[1]] [40] |
| Cost | Zero network | Zero network, modest JS | One network round-trip per resume |
| Trade-off | Lost if page has `unload`/`no-store`/WebSocket | You re-implement what bfcache already does | Refetch may return "stale\" cached-by-server data |

The trap is treating these as alternatives. **Stack them**: keep bfcache eligible (no `unload`, no `no-store` on the HTML, no unnecessary WebSocket on the page), and keep manual scroll restoration as a fallback for unbroken-but-stale cases. On every `pageshow` with `event.persisted === true`, also revalidate critical data - bfcache restores the UI but does not revalidate backend state.

### Tension 2: anti-throttling vs. battery / privacy

Web Workers and Wake Lock both "fix\" idle problems but at a cost. Wake Lock explicitly prevents the OS from turning off the screen, draining battery and, on managed laptops, generating privacy/DLP alerts. Web Workers are quieter but still consume CPU and battery even when the user is not looking. The honest answer for a kiosk is Wake Lock + Workers; for a developer-machine dashboard it is `visibilitychange` refetch alone. The mistake is to bake Wake Lock into a \"general dashboard\" library without a flag - it should always be opt-in.

### Tension 3: "make the server survive closing cmd\" vs. service-management overhead

The ergonomic option (`START /B` + detached spawn) gives the developer what they want with one .cmd edit and zero admin priv. The reliable option (NSSM / pm2-windows-service) requires admin install and a different mental model (services run as SYSTEM, expect path/log configuration). They are not interchangeable: if the user's only requirement is \"don't lose my server when I X-out of the terminal,\" `START /B` is correct; if the requirement includes \"be running tomorrow morning,\" NSSM is correct. Mixing them also serves nobody: shipping `START /B` to a production install is the dominant failure mode of local Node dashboards.

### Cross-cutting observation

The four problems are not really separate problems - they are the same problem (optimizing a long-running, locally hosted SPA) viewed through four browsers, networks, and OS lenses. Every pillar has the same fundamental advice: **survive the lifecycle event** (bfache eligibility, `visibilitychange`, `pageshow.persisted`, process lifetime), and **do not let the browser pause silently** (anti-throttling via Workers, Wake Lock where appropriate, detached process for Node, and explicit revalidation rather than a long cache). The dashboard's job is to ask, at every lifecycle boundary: \"am I still useful, or am I showing stale data?\" - and to ask it cheaply enough that re-asking 60 times per minute is fine.
